summary: Children learn to seriate three or more objects by length and to compare two objects that cannot be placed side by side by using a third object (string or paper strip) as a fixed intermediary length. The underlying reasoning is transitivity: if A is longer than B and B is longer than C, then A is longer than C — and a string kept at one fixed length lets a comparison be carried across a gap. Enactive ordering and carrying an intermediary build the reasoning; recognition formats and static displays can check or summarise it.
misconceptions: Compares only pairs and never chains the inference — insists on placing A directly against C instead of reasoning through the intermediary.
Orders by trial-and-error with no image of an increasing series, and cannot say where a new object should be inserted.
Does not keep the intermediary constant — stretches, re-cuts, or re-aligns the string between the two comparisons.
Non-conservation: believes the string's length changed when it was bent or moved.

activities.title: Carrying a length across a gap with a string
steps: Face two objects (e.g. two cube-towers, or a tall object by the door and a shelf across the room) that are clearly too far apart to bring together and line up.

Hold a fixed length of string against the first object, aligned at the same starting end, and note whether that object is taller or shorter than the string; keep the string's length unchanged for both comparisons (do not change it between the two objects).
Keeping the string uncut and unstretched, carry it across to the second object and see whether it overshoots the top or falls short.

Compare each object to the same string and state the conclusion, voicing the transitive chain — e.g. 'this one is taller than the string; that one is shorter than the string; so this one is taller than that one.'
Try a second far-apart pair to transfer the idea.

Optional screen version: drag a fixed length of string to one tower, then carry it to the other and watch whether it overshoots or falls short, so the transitive step is something the child performs rather than is told.
activities.insight: A string kept at one fixed length can be carried to a place where two objects cannot meet, letting you decide which is longer by comparing each to the same intermediary.

activities.title: Building and extending a seriation staircase
steps: Order three ribbons or cube-towers from shortest to longest using a strategy — pick the shortest, then the next shortest — rather than random swapping.
Progress to ordering five or more into an increasing 'staircase' where each step is the smallest available increase in length.
Check the finished line and fix any inversion (a shorter item placed after a longer one).

Take a new ribbon and decide where it belongs: it goes after every shorter ribbon and before every longer one, so it may land in between two ribbons or at either end if it is the shortest or longest of all.
Optional screen version: drag a fourth ribbon into a staircase that only settles when it sits above the shorter and below the longer neighbour, with a nudge when an inversion is left.
activities.insight: Transitivity becomes the rule that orders a whole set: when no two lengths are equal, each item is longer than everything before it and shorter than everything after, so a new item of a different length from all the others slots into exactly one place (if it matches an existing length, it can go right next to that item).

activities.title: Naming the transitive chain (check and consolidate)
steps: Order a given set of ribbons shortest to longest as an ordering check.
Answer a transitive-inference question in words, e.g. 'The bookshelf is shorter than the string and the door is taller than the string — which is taller?'
Review a staircase display of the 'A > B > C, so A > C' chain, naming each term, as a summary reference after doing the hands-on work.
activities.insight: The transitive conclusion can be stated and recognised in words once it has been built through ordering and carrying an intermediary.

checkQuestion: Give three ribbons of clearly different lengths and say 'Put these in order, shortest to longest.' Then point to a tall object by the door and another across the room that cannot be moved together, hand the child a piece of string, and say: 'Which one is taller? Show me how you can tell.' Watch what they do.
checkAnswer: For the three ribbons, the child builds a correct series — selecting shortest then next-shortest, or checking and fixing inversions. For the two far-apart objects, the child uses the string as an intermediary: matches it to one object, keeps it uncut and aligned at the same end, carries it to the other, and states the conclusion — ideally voicing the transitive link ('this one is taller than the string, that one is shorter than it, so this one is taller').
